sources.text:
by Reagan Reese
Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola unseated Dan S. Sullivan for the state’s U.S. Senate seat, giving Democrats a 56-seat majority in the chamber.
Decision Desk HQ called the race for Peltola on Tuesday evening, with 94% of the votes counted and Peltola holding a 5-point lead over Sullivan, more than 12,000 votes ahead.
The race had a four-way ballot, which included a second Dan Sullivan: independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who received 4,760 votes, according to Decision Desk.
Independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats, congratulated Peltola on her victory.
“Mary understands we must end the war in Iran, overturn Citizens United and tackle the corporate greed destroying our country. Mary. I look forward to working with you,” he said.
Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren noted Peltola is “pro-fish, pro-family, pro-freedom—and now she’s officially flipped Alaska. Congrats, [Mary Peltola]! To every volunteer, donor, organizer, and voter who made this happen: Thank you. Mary, welcome to the Senate. Excited to fight by your side.”
In October, The New York Times reported that Dan J. Sullivan was recruited by people associated with Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC later denied involvement and called the report a “distraction.” President Donald Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and his Justice Department sued to block certification of the race if it could be determined the GOP senator lost because of voter confusion.
Alaska’s chief federal prosecutor opened a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme.
“Every Alaskan deserves a fair election—and they’re going to get one,” U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman said at an October press conference. “Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election will answer for it.”
With Alaska called for Democrats, the winning candidate for Senate majority leader will need 29 votes. The race between New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is the first contested Democrat majority leader race since 1994.
Senate Republicans are quietly pulling for Van Hollen to unseat Schumer, aides and officials told the Daily Signal, because they believe the Maryland senator would take the conference further left and help the GOP draw a contrast with their opponents in 2028.
“This was an affordability election. Van Hollen as leader would be a disaster for Dems in 2028 because their conference would do nothing but woke virtue signaling to the base—open borders, abortion on demand, transgender everything,” one Senate GOP aide told the Daily Signal.
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, where voters select candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of the vote in the first round, tabulation moves to the second round where voters’ second-choice candidates are counted and the worst-performing candidates are eliminated. The process continues until two candidates remain and the leader wins.
– – –
Reagan Reese is the National Political Reporter for the Daily Signal. Zachery Schmidt is the digital editor of The Star News Network and contributed to this story.

Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) has been declared the winner of the Alaska U.S. Senate race, following weeks of ballot counting since Election Day, which President Donald Trump had sought to derail.
The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday night, determining that, with 99 percent of the ballots counted, Peltola had secured around 50.1 percent of the vote. While Alaska employs instant ranked-choice voting, secondary ballot counts will not be necessary, as Peltola secured a majority of votes in the first round of tabulation.
Peltola defeats incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), who garnered just 45.8 percent of the vote. Her victory ensures that Democrats (and aligned independents) will have 56 seats in the Senate, while Republicans will have just 44 members.
While some votes have yet to be counted, the AP explained why it was calling the race.
“Very few ballots remain to be counted, most of which are absentee ballots,” the news outlet said. “Peltola has handily beaten the incumbent Sullivan among absentee votes, which suggests her vote share will remain above 50 percent.”
The result of the race comes despite Trump’s attempts to end vote counting sooner, when it had appeared that Sullivan was closer to Peltola’s totals. The matter was complicated by the fact that a separate Dan Sullivan, running as an independent, had received a few thousand votes, too.
The president, citing a New York Times investigative report that accused the Peltola campaign of recruiting the second Dan Sullivan in an effort to confuse reporters, cried foul in a Truth Social post just two days after Election Day. (The Peltola campaign denies the conclusions drawn from the Times report.)
“The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other ‘slug’ that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over — He easily wins,” Trump wrote in his post. “There is no other fair solution!”
At the time of Trump’s post-election demand, fewer than three-quarters of all votes had even been counted. Had Alaska officials attempted to do what Trump wanted, potentially hundreds of thousands of voters would have been disenfranchised.
Trump had also complained about the other Sullivan candidate before the election. In response, the Department of Justice (DOJ) took the unprecedented action of requesting that Alaska delay certification of the Senate race if the incumbent Sullivan lost.
“It is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the DOJ asserted in its filing.
A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, but the DOJ said that it was going to pursue an appeal. However, due to Peltola’s outright win (without purported “confusion” affecting the race’s outcome), the lawsuit is likely to be dropped, or dismissed again as moot in an appeals court.

sources.news_title: Peltola Beats Sullivan in Alaska; Democrats Reach 56 Seats
sources.text:
Democrat Mary Peltola won Alaska's U.S. Senate race on Tuesday, defeating Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan after news organizations projected her victory two weeks after Election Day. In the latest count, Peltola received 144,302 first-choice votes, or 50.1 percent, to Sullivan's 131,844, or 45.8 percent. Because she cleared a majority in the first round, no ranked-choice tabulation was needed to decide the winner, though state officials had scheduled one for Wednesday in case no candidate topped 50 percent.
Alaska voters can rank up to four candidates, and a candidate who wins a majority of first choices wins outright. The ballot also included Republican Gerald Heikes and a second Dan Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg. Peltola's share exceeded the combined share of her three opponents, which is why the ranked-choice rounds were not expected to change the outcome.
Peltola will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the U.S. Senate and the first Alaska Democrat elected to the chamber since Mark Begich in 2008. She represented the state in the U.S. House from 2022 to 2025 and lost her 2024 reelection bid to Republican Nick Begich III. She entered this race in January at the urging of Senate Democrats and campaigned on affordability, raising money at an unprecedented pace in a contest that also drew record spending.
The race drew heavy national attention because Alaska has long been viewed as a Republican state. President Donald Trump, who carried Alaska in 2024, and Vice President JD Vance held rallies there for Sullivan, who was also backed by Sen. Lisa Murkowski. Peltola led Sullivan in the Aug. 18 primary, 48 percent to 43 percent, and the contest stayed close on Election Night, when early returns showed Sullivan narrowly ahead before Peltola pulled ahead as the count continued.
Her victory gives Democrats 56 seats in the Senate when the new Congress convenes in January, against 44 for Republicans, according to projections by news organizations. Democrats were projected to win control of the chamber on Election Night, before polls closed in Alaska, and Alaska was the last unresolved Senate contest, deciding how large the majority would be rather than who holds it. Republicans currently hold the chamber 53-47. The Democratic gains came in a midterm in which Republicans also lost more than 40 House seats.
The result leaves a pending legal fight in an awkward position. On Oct. 22, at Trump's urging, the Justice Department sued Alaska's Division of Elections in federal court, asking a judge to block certification of the Senate race if Peltola narrowly won. The department argued that Sullivan Jr., who shares the incumbent's name, would divert votes meant for Sen. Sullivan and, under ranked-choice rules, send those votes to Peltola if the race went to additional rounds of tabulation. Trump said he had ordered the lawsuit. A federal judge dismissed it on Nov. 1, finding the government had not established that a ruling could remedy the harm it alleged, and the administration appealed. The status of that appeal was unclear this week.
Peltola's campaign, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and groups including the League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause had sought to join the case, arguing it threatened Peltola's ability to take office even if she won under Alaska's system. The department's suit sought to delay certification only if the second Sullivan's votes could change the ranked-choice result, a condition that Peltola's first-round majority appears to remove.
The namesake candidacy became the most contentious issue in the final days of the race. The New York Times reported late last month that Sullivan Jr.'s candidacy was the product of a sophisticated Democratic recruitment operation, relying largely on a former campaign manager whom Peltola had fired. Peltola has denied involvement in recruiting him. Sen. Sullivan had tried to have the other Sullivan removed from the ballot and warned voters not to cast their votes for the wrong candidate by mistake.
Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., said Tuesday night that Peltola's majority "will probably create issues for the Department of Justice," whose case was built around the possibility of ranked-choice tabulation. Comer also accused Peltola of trying to deceive voters by recruiting what he called a decoy candidate, repeating allegations from the former staffer, and said he was confident she would be seated in the Senate. Sullivan's campaign said before the race was called that it would not concede until the results are certified, arguing that Alaskans deserve a complete and accurate count. A concession from Sullivan had not been announced as of Wednesday afternoon.
Peltola's seat also shapes the Senate Democratic leadership contest. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced last week that he will challenge Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and the caucus votes behind closed doors on Dec. 1. With Alaska counted, the caucus would have 56 members, so a candidate would need 29 votes to win.
Alaska is targeting Nov. 25 to certify its election results, and Peltola is expected to take office when the new Congress convenes in January. The Justice Department's appeal of its dismissed lawsuit remains pending in federal court.

Alaska’s Peltola gives US Senate Dem majority additional cushion
Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Mary Peltola waves to passing motorists on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
WASHINGTON — Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, which The Associated Press called late Tuesday night, sealed Democrats’ unexpected nine pickups in the midterm elections.
Two weeks out from Election Day, the Alaska contest was the last Senate race to be called by The Associated Press. With the flip, Democrats will control 56 seats in the next Congress that begins in January, including two independents who caucus with the party.
Peltola held a 12,458-vote advantage over Sullivan as of Wednesday morning, according to AP.
In another race that was settled days after polls closed Nov. 3, Democrat Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi was called by the AP on Nov. 11. Colom, a district attorney, narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just over 8,000 votes at the time the race was called.
Democrats also flipped Senate seats in the moderate-to-conservative states of Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas.
Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown also wrested back his Senate seat in Ohio, from Republican Sen. John Husted. Because Brown ran in a special election after Husted replaced Vice President JD Vance, he will be sworn in about two weeks before most other senators elected this month.
“Mary Peltola’s victory last night was an exclamation point on what has been a great election year,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Capitol Hill Wednesday.
“We won because we had great candidates, like Peltola,” Schumer added. “We won because we focused on what the American people cared about: lowering their costs, ending corruption, ending the chaos. But now, you know the American people have given us their votes. Now we have to earn their trust. The real work begins today.”
Preliminary results published Tuesday evening by Alaska’s Division of Elections showed Peltola received 50.1% of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, more than enough to avoid a run-off election in the state’s ranked-choice voting system.
Scrutinized race
The race between Peltola and Sullivan drew scrutiny as Republicans alleged Democrats recruited another candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to run as a spoiler candidate.
The two were named on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan, the incumbent senator, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and the U.S. Justice Department launched a legal challenge in late October to preemptively stop the state from certifying the results of the election if, under the state’s ranked-choice voting system, the Republican incumbent Sullivan lost by a smaller margin than the votes earned by Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher.
The New York Times published findings on Oct. 28 that Democratic operatives in Alaska, including in Peltola’s campaign, sought a candidate with the same name. States Newsroom has not independently verified the report. Peltola denied any knowledge of the alleged scheme, according to Alaska Beacon.
The Trump administration’s appeal of the case is pending and was amended to reflect the Times’ report.
Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy was challenged earlier in the year in state court, and Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled in June he could remain on the ballot.
Jennifer Shutt contributed to this report.

OAN Staff Brooke Mallory and Addie Davis
8:44 AM – Wednesday, November 18, 2026
Mary Peltola won the race to become the next United States senator from The Last Frontier, with the midterm election being called two weeks after Election Day.
With 99% of the votes counted, the Associated Press called the race on Tuesday for Peltola (D-Alaska), who received 50.1% of the votes, pushing her past the 50% threshold to win the race outright without going through the Alaska Ranked Choice Voting system. Incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska) garnered 45.8% of the vote.
Democrat Mary Sattler Peltola is a former tribal judge who made history as the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. She grew up in the Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta region and is of Yup’ik descent.
Peltola developed an early connection to natural resource issues, beginning commercial fishing with her family at a young age. Before entering statewide politics, she attended several universities, worked as a fisheries technician for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, and was active in community organizations.
Peltola launched her career in public office in 1998 when she was elected to the Alaska House of Representatives, where she represented the Bethel area until 2009. During her decade in the state legislature, she helped rebuild the bipartisan Bush Caucus, a coalition of rural and off-road community representatives “focused on local infrastructure, education and resource management.”
Following her state legislative service, she held local office on the Bethel City Council, worked as a manager of community development and sustainability for the Donlin Gold project, served as a judge on the Orutsararmiut Native Council Tribal Court, and served as executive director of the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission.
In August 2022, Peltola gained national attention by winning a special election to fill Alaska’s at-large seat in the U.S. House following the death of longtime Congressman Don Young.
She was sworn in as Alaska’s first woman to represent the state in the House and went on to win a full term in the November 2022 general election. During her time in Congress, where she served until January 2025, Peltola served on the House Natural Resources and Transportation and Infrastructure committees.
Incumbent Senator Sullivan ran with the “Complete and Total Endorsement” of President Donald Trump, who issued his unequivocal support in a Truth Social post.
“Senator Dan Sullivan is doing a fantastic job representing the Great People of Alaska! Prior to becoming a very distinguished and Highly Respected Senator, Dan served as State Attorney General and the Commissioner of the Alaska Department of Natural Resources,” Trump wrote in his social media post.
Trump also posted on Truth Social to address a unique ballot issue in the 2026 Alaska primary, where a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan ran against the incumbent. Trump shared a graphic sample ballot on Truth Social telling voters they should check the box specifically for the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, accusing opponents of attempting to confuse voters with the shared name.
Dan S. Sullivan is a politician, attorney, and military veteran currently serving as a junior United States Senator from Alaska. He completed his undergraduate studies in economics at Harvard University before earning a joint law degree and Master of Science in Foreign Service from Georgetown University.
Following graduate school, Sullivan embarked on a distinguished 30-year career in the United States Marine Corps and Marine Corps Reserve, serving as an infantry and reconnaissance officer. His military service included multiple recalls to active duty, notably a deployment to Afghanistan in 2013, before he officially retired from the Marine Corps Reserve with the rank of colonel in February 2024.
Before holding elected office in Alaska, Sullivan built extensive legal and public policy experience at both the federal and state levels. After completing judicial clerkships on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and the Alaska Supreme Court, he worked in private legal practice in Anchorage.
He later served in the administration of President George W. Bush as a director on the National Security Council and National Economic Council, followed by his appointment as U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Economic, Energy, and Business Affairs. Returning to state leadership, then-Governor Sarah Palin appointed Sullivan as Alaska Attorney General in 2009.
He subsequently served as Commissioner of the Alaska Department of Natural Resources under then-Governor Sean Parnell, managing the state’s vast energy, mineral, timber, and land development interests.
In 2014, Sullivan was elected to the United States Senate after defeating incumbent Democrat Senator Mark Begich, and he earned a second term in 2020 by winning reelection against independent challenger Al Gross.
In the Senate, he sits on key panels vital to his state’s priorities, including the Armed Services, Commerce, Science, and Transportation, Environment and Public Works, and Veterans’ Affairs committees. His legislative efforts focus heavily on expanding Alaskan energy production, upgrading Arctic defense infrastructure, advocating for veterans, supporting maritime industries and combating domestic violence. Sullivan resides in Anchorage with his wife, Julie Fate Sullivan, with whom he has three daughters.
Daniel James “Dan J.” Sullivan Jr. is a former U.S. Forest Service employee and retired fifth-grade teacher based in Petersburg, Alaska.
He entered the 2026 U.S. Senate election in Alaska as a candidate. Following state administrative reviews and court challenges regarding voter confusion over his sharing a name with the incumbent, state election authorities listed him on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. with No Party Affiliation.
A late-October report from The New York Times revealed that campaign staffers for Peltola and allied operatives allegedly worked to recruit candidates with the same name as Senator Dan Sullivan to run in the race in order to cause confusion and pull votes away from the incumbent. The report also alleged that Gerald L. Heikes (R-Alaska), who ran in the 2026 Senate race, had said he had been recruited into the election “by a guy from the Midwest.”
The NYT said the article was based on interviews with 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were potential candidates the team tried to recruit. Extensive interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager were included in the reporting, and the outlet said it obtained dozens of text messages regarding the effort.
Heikes, also known as “Tap,” is a member of the Republican Party based in Alaska. He has maintained a recurring presence in Alaskan electoral politics over several cycles, running for various state and federal offices.
His platform generally emphasizes conservative principles, including the protection of private property rights, free-enterprise economics, and reduced government regulation.
Throughout his political career, Heikes has frequently entered Republican primary contests and nonpartisan primary elections across Alaska. His candidacy history includes runs for Governor of Alaska as well as multiple campaigns for Alaska’s single congressional district in the U.S. House.
Despite operating as a perennial grassroots candidate without high-profile endorsements or extensive institutional party backing, Heikes continues to participate regularly in Alaskan primary ballots.
Following Tuesday’s election, Trump asserted that votes for the “Fake Dan Sullivan” and Heikes should be given to the “REAL Dan Sullivan,” stating there “is no other fair solution” in a November 5th Truth Social post.
The day after the midterm elections, Peltola led incumbent Dan Sullivan by only 637 votes, though that gap widened to about 12,500 votes by Tuesday, November 17th, according to the AP. Combined, Heikes and Dan J. Sullivan Jr. received less than 11,000 votes with 99% of the vote counted.
If no candidate received a majority of votes under Alaska’s Ranked Choice Voting system, the candidate with the fewest votes would be eliminated, and the voters who cast their ballots for that individual would then have their votes go to their second choices, according to the Alaska Division of Elections. The process is then repeated until one candidate receives a majority of votes.

Her victory gave Democrats a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate after the party captured nine Republican-held seats during the November midterm elections.
According to Alaska Public Media’s election coverage, approximately 99% of ballots had been counted when the race was called. Although overseas absentee ballots could continue arriving through Wednesday, Nov. 18, election analysts determined that Sullivan could no longer overcome Peltola’s lead.
The victory makes Peltola the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Alaska since 2008 and the first Alaska Native person elected to the chamber.
However, the result does not end the controversy surrounding the candidacy of retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who entered the Senate race sharing nearly the same name as the Republican incumbent.
An Oct. 28 investigation by The New York Times reported that political operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee worked to recruit candidates who could divert votes from the Republican senator.
The investigation cited interviews, internal communications and documents indicating that campaign personnel searched for Alaska residents named Dan Sullivan and approached potential candidates about entering the race.
According to the reporting, the effort extended beyond Daniel J. Sullivan and involved attempts to encourage other candidates to run against the incumbent.
Gerald Heikes, another Republican candidate who appeared on the November ballot, was also reportedly recruited as part of the effort.
Peltola has denied knowing about or participating in the recruitment of another Dan Sullivan.
Speaking to supporters in Juneau before Election Day, she rejected allegations that she was involved in an effort to confuse voters.
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola said.
Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, has also denied that his candidacy was coordinated with Peltola’s campaign.
He maintained that he entered the election legitimately and had a right to run under his legal name.
The controversy began months before the general election.
Daniel J. Sullivan filed his candidacy in May, prompting complaints from the incumbent senator and Alaska Republicans that his participation could mislead voters.
The Alaska Division of Elections initially determined that his candidacy was not genuine and attempted to exclude him from the ballot.
However, an Alaska Superior Court judge overturned that decision in June, ruling that state election officials had imposed a good-faith candidacy requirement that was not supported by applicable law.
The Alaska Supreme Court subsequently upheld the decision allowing Daniel J. Sullivan to compete.
State officials differentiated the two candidates on the ballot by identifying the incumbent as Dan S. Sullivan and listing the other candidate as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
The incumbent also received an official designation identifying him as the sitting senator.
Alaska’s election system allows the top four candidates in a nonpartisan primary to advance to the general election, where voters rank candidates in order of preference.
In the August primary, Peltola received approximately 49.5% of the vote, followed by Sen. Sullivan with 41.4%. Daniel J. Sullivan received approximately 2.5%, while Heikes received about 1%.
The controversy escalated in October after The New York Times published its investigation into the alleged recruitment operation.
President Donald Trump accused Democrats of attempting to manipulate the election and called for Peltola and those involved in the alleged effort to face criminal prosecution.
On Oct. 22, the Justice Department filed a federal lawsuit seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying an election result if Sen. Sullivan lost by fewer votes than Daniel J. Sullivan received.
The department argued that a narrow defeat could indicate that voter confusion had affected the outcome.
According to FactCheck.org’s examination of the dispute, the lawsuit asked the court to delay certification while officials investigated whether votes cast for the similarly named candidate were intended for the incumbent senator.
The federal government argued that the presence of two candidates with nearly identical names could undermine election integrity.
Peltola’s campaign and other parties challenged the lawsuit, maintaining that federal authorities lacked a legal basis to interfere with Alaska’s certification process.
On Nov. 1, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the Justice Department’s case, finding that the government had not established grounds for the requested intervention.
The department appealed to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, where the case remains pending.
Meanwhile, federal prosecutors opened a separate criminal investigation into the recruitment allegations.
U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman confirmed the existence of a grand jury investigation shortly before Election Day. Federal authorities have reportedly issued subpoenas, preservation notices and target letters to individuals they believe may have information about the recruitment operation.
According to The Washington Post’s Nov. 17 reporting, the Justice Department intends to continue examining the allegations despite Peltola’s victory.
Attorney General Todd Blanche previously said that investigating potential election fraud would remain a priority regardless of which candidate won.
The investigation has involved political operatives and attorneys associated with the Democratic campaign, including individuals connected to voting rights attorney Marc Elias’ law firm.
Elias has criticized the investigation as politically motivated, while federal officials have maintained that they are examining potential violations of election law.
Alaska Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy also ordered a state investigation following publication of the recruitment allegations.
Separately, Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., chairman of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, requested records and communications from individuals allegedly involved in the effort.
Johnson described the allegations as a potential attempt to undermine the integrity of Alaska’s Senate election.
No criminal conviction or final judicial finding has established that Peltola participated in an unlawful recruitment scheme.
The final vote totals also complicate claims that the similarly named candidates determined the election’s outcome.
According to Alaska Public Media, Peltola received nearly 1,600 more votes than the combined total cast for Sen. Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan and Heikes.
Daniel J. Sullivan received fewer than 5,000 votes, substantially less than Peltola’s margin of more than 12,000 votes over the incumbent.
Consequently, the reported results do not support the claim that transferring every vote cast for the other Sullivan to the incumbent would have reversed the outcome.
Peltola also crossed the 50% threshold on first-choice ballots, meaning no ranked-choice redistribution was necessary.
Her victory concludes a political comeback following her defeat in Alaska’s 2024 U.S. House election.
Peltola first entered Congress in 2022 after winning a special election to fill the seat previously held by Republican Rep. Don Young.
She became the first Alaska Native woman elected to Congress and subsequently won a full House term before losing reelection to Republican Nick Begich in 2024.
During her Senate campaign, Peltola emphasized affordability, energy costs, fisheries management and Alaska’s relationship with the federal government.
Her campaign slogan, “fish, family, freedom,” reflected her focus on issues affecting rural communities, including declining salmon populations and the rising cost of living.
Following the Senate race call, Peltola thanked voters and pledged to address economic concerns.
“Over the course of this campaign I’ve spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table,” she said in a statement reported by The Associated Press.
“Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first.”
Sullivan, a Marine Corps veteran and former Alaska attorney general, was first elected to the Senate in 2014.
He campaigned on strengthening national defense, expanding domestic energy production and supporting Trump’s economic and security policies.
His campaign declined to immediately concede following the election, saying it wanted the counting and certification process to be completed.
Alaska’s official certification is scheduled for Nov. 25.
The Justice Department’s appeal remains pending, although the current briefing schedule extends into January, after the new Congress is scheduled to convene.
The criminal investigation into the alleged recruitment effort is also continuing independently of the election certification process.
Peltola’s victory completes the final unresolved Senate contest of the 2026 midterms, giving Democrats a 56-seat majority when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3, 2027.
The election result stands separately from the ongoing investigations, which have not produced a finding establishing that the alleged recruitment operation changed the outcome or that Peltola personally engaged in unlawful conduct.

Peltola wins Alaska US Senate seat, giving Democrats a 56 seat majority
Mary Peltola greets supporters on election night, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at a Mary Peltola watch party in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
Alaskans have elected Mary Peltola, a Democrat, to one of the state’s two U.S. Senate seats. She will replace incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, according to preliminary, partial election results published Tuesday by the Alaska Division of Elections.
Peltola will return to Congress as the 56th Democrat in the U.S. Senate when it convenes in January after a tsunami of pro-Democratic election results saw Republicans evicted from the Senate’s governing majority.
She was the first Alaska Native woman to serve in Congress when she was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2022 and will be the one of the first Indigenous people to serve in the U.S. Senate.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she wrote on Facebook on Tuesday evening. “Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”
With 209,003 ballots counted through Tuesday evening, Peltola had 50.1% of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, more than enough to avoid a ranked choice runoff election.
The Associated Press called the Senate race for Peltola shortly after elections officials confirmed she had more than 50% of the vote.
Sullivan had 45.8% of the first-choice votes, followed by Republican challenger Gerald Heikes with 2.1% and independent challenger Dan J. Sullivan with 1.7%.
Final preliminary results are expected Wednesday, and the Division of Elections is planning to publish a certified result on Nov. 25.
In a statement issued Monday morning, Sullivan campaign spokesman Nate Adams said that “Alaskans deserve a complete and accurate count, and we will let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified. The Division of Elections has work left to do, and we respect the Alaskans doing it. We will not be commenting on individual ballot updates or outside projections in the meantime.”
Peltola’s participation in the Senate race wasn’t a surprise: National Democrats tried to recruit her as far back as 2025, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer playing a key role.
After announcing her run for office in January, Peltola campaigned with the slogan “Fish, Family, Freedom,” emphasizing an anticorruption platform, limits on commercial trawl fisheries and a politically moderate stance that includes support for development and oil and gas drilling on federal land in Alaska.
One of 16 candidates in the August primary election, the former Alaska U.S. House Representative instantly became Sullivan’s leading challenger.
Another candidate, Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, immediately drew public attention for having the same first and last name as Sen. Sullivan.
The Alaska Division of Elections ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible to run, citing irregularities in his candidacy that indicated he was running only to confuse voters, but Dan J. Sullivan appealed the decision and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in his favor.
Dan J. Sullivan finished third in the primary. Fourth-place primary election finisher David Leslie, a progressive Democrat, withdrew after the final result. That promoted Heikes into the general election and concentrated the Democratic vote around Peltola.
Republican and Democratic campaigners collectively spent more than $100 million to promote Peltola and Sen. Sullivan, making it the most expensive election campaign in state history. Final tallies won’t be available until early next year.
Shortly before the primary, Peltola fired her campaign manager, Elisa Rios, and made other major staffing moves. Rios subsequently told the New York Times that Peltola was physically and verbally abusive toward staff and was a key source in a Times article that said Democratic campaigners worked to recruit independent Dan J. Sullivan as a spoiler candidate to help Peltola defeat Sen. Sullivan.
Peltola herself has denied knowing about the recruitment, but Republican officials — including President Donald Trump — have called for legal action against Peltola and her campaign.
The FBI and the Alaska Department of Public Safety are investigating whether Democratic campaigners committed a legal violation. No charges have been filed.
The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil lawsuit against the Division of Elections, seeking to prevent it from certifying Peltola as the winner of the election, but a federal judge in Alaska dismissed the case. That ruling is now on appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
Part of the federal case was based on the idea that confused voters might have chosen Dan J. Sullivan instead of Sen. Sullivan. Peltola now has more votes than both Sullivans combined.

It is the ninth Senate seat the Democrats have taken from Republicans in the midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
The Democrats also won back the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.
Peltola defeated the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S Sullivan, who is yet to comment.

She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Donald Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but defeat for the Republicans in this year's Senate race in the state caps off a string of losses in the midterms for the president's party.
Many voters across the United States cited cost-of-living issues as a factor that affected how they cast their ballots.

The final unresolved U.S. Senate race of 2026 has finally been called, and Democrats will begin the next Congress with a 56-44 advantage in the chamber.
The Associated Press called Alaska for Democrat Mary Peltola on Tuesday night, giving her the victory over two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola’s win represents the ninth Democratic Senate flip of the midterms and closes out an election that dramatically reshaped the balance of power in Washington. That final number also puts a clearer starting point on the 2028 Senate map we looked at yesterday. Republicans will enter the next cycle with 44 seats, meaning they need a net gain of six seats to reach a 50-50 Senate and seven to reach an outright 51-seat majority.
Peltola Wins After a Controversial Race
Alaska was never just another close Senate contest. The race drew national attention because there were two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot, including Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and retired Petersburg teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
Alaska Senate vote count as of AP’s Nov. 18 race call:
- Mary Peltola (D): 144,302 votes — 50.12%
- Dan S. Sullivan (R): 131,844 votes — 45.80%
- Gerald L. Heikes (R): 6,105 votes — 2.12%
- Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. (I): 4,760 votes — 1.65%
- Write-ins: 885 votes — 0.31%
That second candidacy became a major controversy after New York Times reporting found that Democratic operatives had worked to recruit spoiler candidates who could complicate the incumbent’s path. Sullivan Jr. received support from thousands of voters, while ranked-choice records suggested many Peltola voters placed him second. Mississippi Went Democratic Too
The other long-running Senate count ended a week earlier. AP called Mississippi for Democrat Scott Colom on Nov. 11, giving Democrats their 55th seat at the time. We had been tracking both races in our earlier Alaska and Mississippi Senate update.
With Alaska now settled, both of the final outstanding races ended as Democratic pickups. That locks in the incoming Senate at 56 Democrats and 44 Republicans and puts a hard number on the challenge facing the GOP in 2028.
The 2028 Math Is Now Clear
Republicans will have opportunities next cycle. North Carolina and Wisconsin are the most obvious Republican-held seats Democrats will target, while the GOP will look toward Democratic seats in Arizona, Georgia, Nevada and Pennsylvania. But Republicans are not starting one or two seats away from control.
They need six net pickups simply to get the chamber back to 50-50, where control would depend on the vice president, and seven for an outright majority. That is the baseline after a 2026 election in which Democrats flipped nine Republican Senate seats.
Alaska was the last race left on the board. Now that it is finally called, the 2026 Senate map is complete and the size of the Republican climb in 2028 is no longer theoretical.

Former Representative Mary Peltola has flipped a crucial seat.
Senator-elect Mary Peltola

Senator-elect Mary Peltola
Democratic challenger Mary Peltola has unseated Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
The former Alaska representative defeated Sullivan with 50.1 percent of the vote, with 99 percent of the votes counted. The AP finally called the race Tuesday night after weeks of counting. She will be one of the first two Native women in the U.S. Senate, alongside Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.
Peltola entered the race in January with a focus on fishing, an Alaska-specific policy area that touches everything from affordability to labor and money in politics. She won with the slogan, “Fish, Family, and Freedom.”
The Democrat’s victory comes after the Justice Department sued to block Alaska from certifying its Senate election results in the event that the incumbent Sullivan lost due to voter “confusion” because there was another Republican named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot.
Alaska’s Supreme Court in June upheld lower court rulings that found the two Sullivans could run in the same election—but the Trump administration waited until just days before the election to intervene. What’s more, a closer look at Alaska’s ballots showed that Sullivan was clearly listed as the “(Registered Republican) Incumbent.”
The incumbent Sullivan was seeking a third term with the endorsement of President Donald Trump, who carried the state by 13 points in 2024. But as Trump’s behavior has become more outrageous, the president’s support morphed into a liability.
Peltola’s victory gives Democrats a whopping 56 seats in the Senate.
Trump’s Answer to Election Bloodbath Is Even More Renovations
Food and gas prices are still high, but Donald Trump wants more granite at the White House.
Tasos Katopodis/Gettyimages
Americans turned out en masse on Election Day to vote against the Iran war and the rising cost of living, according to an analysis by senior administration officials. But rather than address public concern, Donald Trump has decided to orient his focus back toward his Washington vanity projects.
The president is breaking ground on even more construction, including spending $3 million to repave Lafayette Square and an extension to the black granite walkway he installed around the West Wing earlier this year, The Washington Post reported Tuesday.
Yet this time, the National Park Service is expected to foot the bill, according to insiders who spoke with the Post.
The White House instructed the Post to speak with the Interior Department for an official statement on the matter. The department eventually told the paper that Trump was working to fix “obvious blight” that had supposedly festered under previous, apparently neglectful administrations.
“Not only is President Donald J. Trump using his expert builder experience to make the White House beautiful now, he’s improving and restoring the grounds to greatness for future presidents to enjoy,” the department said in a statement. “President Trump should be thanked for making our nation’s capital better than how he found it.”
Trump has obsessed over his legacy throughout his second term rather than address genuine national issues, a fixation easily illustrated by the long list of vanity projects he’s cooked up instead of fulfilling the difficult job of steering the nation. Beyond the work on the new walkways, Trump has razed the White House East Wing to build a $600 million ballroom (the price of which keeps growing), advanced efforts to build a 250-foot “Triumphal Arch,” gutted the Lincoln bathroom, transformed the Palm Room from a lush green foyer into a sterile lobby, and mowed down Jackie Kennedy’s famous Rose Garden.
The administration also spent more than $16 million on an unsuccessful and rushed renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, took a sledgehammer to the Harry S. Truman Bowling Alley, indiscriminately axed trees in the Washington area, and destroyed the Kennedy Center.

Video of the brutal arrest shows the woman’s husband shouting at agents that she is pregnant.
CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP/Getty Images
A U.S. citizen was pepper-sprayed and thrown on the ground by federal immigration agents on Sunday, even after she warned them that she was pregnant.
Lizbeth Vargas Andrade and some of her family members were monitoring federal immigration agents’ activity outside Stanislaus County Jail in Modesto, California, when ICE blocked her sister-in-law Monica Alvarado’s vehicle. Moments later, ICE agents can be seen throwing her to the ground on her stomach, and cuffing her hands behind her back.
Vargas Andrade was taken by ICE and detained for several hours before being released, her attorney told ABC News. She visited a hospital, where doctors determined that her baby was unharmed. One other person who was riding in Alvarado’s car was detained by ICE.

During the agency’s sweeping enforcement operation in Minneapolis earlier this year, ICE agents violently restrained a woman, dragging her through the snow and pinning her face down as onlookers shouted that the woman was pregnant. Representative Beth Van Duyne doesn’t want the public to assume the worst.

Texas GOP Representative Beth Van Duyne thinks that the release of the new iPhone—not a cyberattack—could be responsible for the slew of network outages that have afflicted the U.S. in the month of November.
“We’re getting reports that Apple is now the latest in the list of disruptions after we saw banking and Microsoft, the ground stop.… What is your reaction, and can you give us any more information on the cause of some of these?” Newsmax’s Bianca de la Garza asked Van Duyne, who worked for the Department of Housing and Urban Development in the first Trump administration before being elected to Congress.

The possibility of a cyberattack is a reasonable question to raise when multiple large banks, Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, the National Security Agency, and several other technology services have all experienced outages in the past few days. Users reported outages on Apple platforms, as well as for Charles Schwab and Gmail.

Even more companies experienced major system disruptions on Tuesday, following a string of technology outages that have sparked panic and confusion among Americans.
Apple said that it was addressing problems with its systems after an internal update caused some brief outages, The New York Times reported Tuesday.

Apple’s system status webpage showed there were also issues with AppleCare, Apple Business, and the App Store. At Apple stores in New York City and Chicago, employees told NBC News that they had been unable to complete sales or make appointments.
Charles Schwab, a financial services company, said it had resolved an issue that temporarily downed its website Tuesday, just one day after major banks such as JP Morgan Chase and Bank of America were hit by outages.
Gmail also appeared to experience an outage Tuesday, according to Downdetector, which tracks problems with widely used technology platforms.
If people are looking to the Trump administration for answers, they may want to look elsewhere. Speaking on Fox News Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he was 98 percent sure that these outages weren’t the results of cyberattacks, but rather than provide answers, he simply spun his own theories. sources.news_title: Mary Peltola Wins Alaska Senate Race After Campaign Allegedly Recruited Another Dan Sullivan
sources.text:
Former Democratic Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola defeated Republican Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan Tuesday after recruiting another Republican candidate with the same name to boost her chances, The Associated Press reported.
Aides with Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) worked to recruit candidates to run as Republicans to take votes away from Sullivan, which prompted a candidate with the same name to join the race, The New York Times first reported. Alaska’s open voting system made this scheme possible because candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without party vetting.
Former schoolteacher Dan J. Sullivan joined in May just three days before the June 1 deadline. Democratic strategist Amber Lee authored a press release announcing the other Sullivan’s candidacy, metadata reviewed by the DCNF showed.
The DSCC introduced a veteran Democratic operative named Jerid Kurtz to former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios and former chief of staff Anton McParland, according to the Times. Kurtz reportedly spoke on the phone with a Peltola campaign aide to say he had just arrived in Petersburg, where the other Sullivan lives. (RELATED: Other Dan Sullivan Advances To General Election Against Incumbent Dan Sullivan)
Peltola visited the other Sullivan’s hometown on May 28, days before he filed to launch his candidacy, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher informed Sullivan in an Aug. 26 letter that his declaration of candidacy “was not filed in order to declare an actual good-faith candidacy,” but rather to confuse voters into voting for the wrong Sullivan. After Sullivan appealed the ruling, Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled he could remain on the ballot for the state’s primary.
The Alaska Supreme Court overturned that ruling in a June 30 decision and allowed the other Sullivan to be on the ballot. The DSCC and Peltola’s campaign celebrated the high court’s decision, according to the Times.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a lawsuit to block Alaska’s Senate results if the incumbent senator loses. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason, an Obama-appointed judge, blocked the lawsuit Sunday, arguing that the DOJ failed to explain what authority it brought the charges under and how the alleged fraud could be addressed.
The DOJ issued at least three dozen subpoenas Thursday as part of its investigation into Peltola’s alleged scheme.
The other Sullivan changed his party affiliation from Republican to unaffiliated eight days before the general election. Former Democratic Alaska Senate candidate David Leslie told the Times that Kurtz urged him to drop out of the race after advancing to the general election, according to the Times. Kurtz allegedly told Leslie he was “proud” of his decision to leave the race in a text message.
Sullivan and Peltola were neck-and-neck after Alaska voters soured on the incumbent senator and Trump, according to Data for Progress. Voters overwhelmingly disapproved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war and the economy as the prices of gas, food and other goods remained high.
President Donald Trump won Alaska in 2024 by a 54.5% to 41.4% margin and Sullivan won his 2020 race by 12.7 points.

sources.news_title: Democrats pick up another U.S. Senate seat with win in Alaska
sources.text: JUNEAU, Alaska — Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins. The Alaska race was the last U.S. Senate contest to be resolved in this year’s midterm elections and gave Democrats a 56-44 majority after they flipped nine GOP-held seats to retake the chamber. The party also won campaigns in other conservative states, including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi. In a statement, Peltola said voters sent a clear message that “the status quo in D.C. is not working for Alaska.” “Over the course of this campaign I’ve spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table,” she said. “Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first.” Sullivan spokesperson Nate Adams did not respond to a request for comment. Adams had said Monday that the campaign would let the process “run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.” A spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee also did not respond. As part of the Nov. 3 general election, Alaskans also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, as former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by Trump. The Associated Press has not yet called the U.S. House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich. Flipping Alaska’s seat was pivotal to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate Peltola previously held the state’s lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026. In the campaign’s final stretch, however, she faced allegations that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent. Trump called for Peltola’s prosecution after The New York Times first reported the allegation less than a week before the Nov. 3 election. Peltola denied any involvement. “I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau days before the election. Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign or running at the Democrats’ behest. He has not responded to messages from The Associated Press since The Times’ article was published. Candidacy of second Dan Sullivan roiled the race The Times report was based partly on text messages and other documents and interviews with a former Peltola campaign manager, who was fired shortly before this year’s open primary and later sought to recant her statements. But the second Sullivan had already been on Trump’s mind. He referred to him multiple times during a rally in support of the senator in mid-October. The U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit that Trump said he ordered. It sought to block certification of the race if the incumbent were to lose, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Peltola called the lawsuit “flagrant corruption.” The case was dismissed by a federal judge, but the Justice Department appealed. Attorneys for the state sought dismissal, saying officials should be able to conduct the election “without unwarranted interference by the United States.” They also argued the ballot was designed to distinguish the two Sullivans as much as possible and that Alaska’s ranked choice voting process would allow any voters who might be confused to rank them. The Justice Department also confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska’s U.S. attorney would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into. Peltola finished first in the primary with 49.5 per cent of the vote, followed by the incumbent with 41.4 per cent. Dan J. Sullivan finished a distant third with about 2.5 per cent, but he advanced to the general election as one of the top four finishers. He was listed on both ballots as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation, while the senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent. Peltola played up her rural roots during the campaign During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are generally only accessible by air or water. Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to separate herself from national Democrats and build a coalition of support around a platform of “Alaska first.” “Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said. “I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.” The strategy resonated with voters who felt they could relate to Peltola, who is Yup’ik and often spoke about growing up in western Alaska. “People across the country don’t understand what it means to grow up in a place where there isn’t running water, where there’s only one store, where gas costs US$17 a gallon, where heating fuel is not a guaranteed thing, which means that your house isn’t necessarily going to be warm when it’s 50 below zero,” Sam Schimmel, who is Alaska Native, said in Anchorage after Peltola’s win. “Having somebody who really understands what that means in D.C., representing us in the Senate, is an enormous achievement,” he added and also noted the significance of Peltola’s election as the first Alaska Native in the Senate. Michael Dunn, also in Anchorage, said he voted for Sullivan but hopes Peltola does well. “She put in the effort,” he said of her campaign. “So hopefully she puts in the effort in D.C. for us.” Peltola emphasized affordability issues “Lower 48” became something of an insult bandied by both sides. Sullivan tried to align Peltola with “Lower 48 liberals” who want to restrict oil and gas drilling, mining and other resource development in the state. Peltola said that while she would work with Trump to get things done for Alaska, “I will never put any Lower 48 politician before Alaskans. That’s the difference between Dan and me.” Emphasizing her Alaska roots, she spoke about fishing for salmon on the Kuskokwim River with her father and spending parts of the summer at fish camp with her children and late husband, who died in September 2023. She said the fish and wildlife Alaskans long relied on to fill their freezers for the winter were becoming harder to find. The changes were forcing people to buy more food and other staples at the store — supplies that must be barged or flown in — and deal with “crushing prices,” she said. Peltola also said she saw members of Congress who were “more focused on their stock portfolios” than helping ease those costs and vowed to push back against the billionaire class. She will be just the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate. The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014. ___ Becky Bohrer, The Associated Press Associated Press journalist Mark Thiessen in Anchorage contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Mary Peltola ousts incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate race, giving Democrats 56 seats
sources.text:
(CNN) — Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola will defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s Senate race, picking up a hotly contested seat for Democrats in a GOP-leaning state.
Peltola blocked Sullivan’s bid for a third term after a nationally watched battle that brought President Donald Trump to Alaska and featured a spirited debate over who was best positioned to meet the unique needs of the massive, remote state. The race was upended by a spoiler candidate with the same name as the incumbent, drawing legal action by the Trump administration and casting uncertainty over whether the election would be certified if Peltola won.
Peltola, who is of Yup’ik descent, is poised to become the first Native American senator from Alaska, as well as one of the first female Native American senators from anywhere in the country. She will share the latter title with Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s Democratic lieutenant governor who was just elected to her state’s open Senate seat.
The Alaska race became a crucial part of Democrats’ majority math after Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer recruited Peltola to attempt a political comeback in a state that Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. After the blue wave that swept the midterms, Democrats will now hold 56 seats in the chamber come January.
Schumer celebrated Peltola’s victory in a statement, saying that a 56-seat majority was “an unimaginable result even just a few months ago.” He added that Democrats are now “in a prime position to create a durable majority that can create lasting, real results for the American people.”
In her own statement, Peltola said her election sent the message that the “status quo in DC is not working for Alaska.”
Peltola held Alaska’s at-large House seat from 2022 to 2025, serving as the state’s first Native American elected to Congress. While she lost reelection in 2024 to Republican Nick Begich, she significantly outperformed her party’s performance in the presidential election that year.
This year’s Senate contest had a unique twist in that another Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher, qualified for the ballot and advanced to the general election, threatening to siphon off GOP support from the incumbent. Republicans accused Democrats of recruiting the other Sullivan to confuse voters, a charge the party denied.
Days before the election, the Trump administration took the remarkable step of filing a lawsuit to block certification of the election if the incumbent loses, citing the confusion that the other Dan Sullivan could cause.
Soon after, the New York Times reported that Democratic operatives working on behalf of Peltola had recruited the second Dan Sullivan, intensifying the partisan battle over the spoiler candidate. While Peltola’s campaign continued to deny involvement in the other Dan Sullivan’s run, Alaska GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy launched an investigation into the efforts outlined in the Times story, and Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted and removed from the ballot.
A federal judge dismissed the administration’s lawsuit over the election in early November, though the Department of Justice has filed a notice to appeal. Dunleavy has raised the possibility the state could withhold certification of the election while its investigation is underway.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance separately visited Alaska in the final weeks of the election campaign to support Sullivan, who pitched himself as a more effective lawmaker than Peltola was in Congress. Sullivan sought to tie Peltola to national Democratic figures, including former President Joe Biden, and railed against “lower 48 liberals” whom he said did not understand Alaska’s unique way of life.
Running on a campaign slogan of “fish, family and freedom,” Peltola distanced herself from her party at the national level, promoting herself as more supportive of border security, gun rights and the oil-and-gas industry. She also ran ads pushing back against Republican attacks on her position on transgender rights, saying, “No, I don’t want kids getting surgeries to change genders or men in girls’ bathrooms.”
Peltola’s campaign was shaken in September by a New York Times report alleging staff mistreatment, including that she shoved an aide in one outburst. Peltola’s campaign denied a pattern of abusing her staff but said she “sometimes struggled to deal with her grief” after the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023.
Sullivan was first elected to the Senate in 2014. He previously was commissioner of the Alaska Department of Natural Resources and the state attorney general.
This story and headline have been updated with additional information.

By CNBCTV18.com November 18, 2026, 5:33:21 PM IST (Published)
Democrats have flipped nine Republican-held US Senate seats in the 2026 midterm elections, marking their biggest Senate gain in nearly 70 years. The v...Read More
1/9
Mary Peltola, Alaska: Peltola defeated Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, securing the ninth and final Democratic Senate pickup. Peltola, who previously represented Alaska in the House, won after crossing the 50% threshold, avoiding a ranked-choice runoff. (Image: Reuters)
2/9
Josh Turek, Iowa: Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson to flip Iowa’s Senate seat, becoming the first Democrat to win a statewide federal race in Iowa since Barack Obama in 2008. A state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, Turek was born with spina bifida and campaigned on lowering costs for farmers, healthcare and fighting corruption. His victory was particularly significant in a state Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024, and marked a major Democratic breakthrough in rural America. (Image: Reuters)
3/9
Adam Hamilton, Kansas: Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor, pulled off a stunning upset over Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Kansas in 94 years. His victory ended the longest Senate losing streak for Democrats in the country and flipped a seat that had been considered safely Republican. Hamilton campaigned as an “independent-minded Democrat” on affordability, healthcare and political unity. (Image: Reuters)
4/9
Troy Jackson, Maine: Jackson pulled off one of the cycle’s biggest upsets, defeating five-term Republican Senator Susan Collins and ending her nearly 30-year Senate career. A former logger and Maine Senate president from rural Aroostook County, Jackson became the Democratic nominee only about 100 days before the election after the original nominee, Graham Platner, withdrew. Jackson campaigned on workers’ rights, healthcare and the cost of living, while portraying Collins as too aligned with President Donald Trump. His victory was also historic: Maine had not voted out a sitting US senator since 1978. (Image: Reuters)
5/9
Scott Colom, Mississippi: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a narrow upset, becoming Mississippi’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction. Colom is also the first Black senator from the state to be elected directly by voters; Mississippi’s previous Black senators, Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce, were chosen by the state legislature during Reconstruction. (Image: Reuters)
6/9
Roy Cooper, North Carolina | Former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper defeated Republican candidate Michael Whatley in the Senate race. Cooper won by a comfortable margin of nearly 20 percentage points, flipping a Republican-held seat in a state that has become a major battleground. (Image: Reuters)
7/9
Sherrod Brown, Ohio: Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown returned to the Senate after defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a special election. Brown won about 50% of the vote, reclaiming a seat Democrats lost in the 2024 election. (Image: Reuters)
8/9
Annie Andrews, South Carolina: Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina, delivering one of the cycle’s biggest surprises. Andrews won about 51% of the vote and flipped a Republican-held seat in a state that has voted reliably Republican in recent presidential elections. (Image: Reuters)
9/9
James Talarico, Texas: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, resulting in one of the most significant Democratic Senate pickups of the cycle. Talarico won roughly 55% of the vote, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans. (Image: Reuters)

sources.news_title: Peltola elected to fill Alaska U.S. Senate seat, becomes Senate’s 56th Democrat nationally
sources.text:
Peltola elected to fill Alaska U.S. Senate seat, becomes Senate’s 56th Democrat nationally
Alaskans have elected Mary Peltola, a Democrat, to one of the state’s two U.S. Senate seats. She will replace incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, according to preliminary, partial election results published Tuesday by the Alaska Division of Elections.
Peltola will return to Congress as the 56th Democrat in the U.S. Senate when it convenes in January after a tsunami of pro-Democratic election results saw Republicans evicted from the Senate’s governing majority.
She was the first Alaska Native woman to serve in Congress when she was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2022 and will be the one of the first Indigenous people to serve in the U.S. Senate.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she wrote on Facebook on Tuesday evening. “Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”
With 209,003 ballots counted through Tuesday evening, Peltola had 50.1% of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, more than enough to avoid a ranked choice runoff election.
How Alaska elections work
In Alaska, all candidates for an office run together in an August primary election, and voters pick their favorite candidate. The top four vote-getters advance to the November general election.
If there are four or fewer candidates, all advance to November.
In November, voters rank the four candidates in order of preference. If one candidate has more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they win. If none have 50%, the person with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and their votes are redistributed to their voters’ second choices.
Eliminations and redistributions continue until two candidates are left. The person with the most votes wins.
The Associated Press called the Senate race for Peltola shortly after elections officials confirmed she had more than 50% of the vote.
Sullivan had 45.8% of the first-choice votes, followed by Republican challenger Gerald Heikes with 2.1% and independent challenger Dan J. Sullivan with 1.7%.
Final preliminary results are expected Wednesday, and the Division of Elections is planning to publish a certified result on November 25.
In a statement issued Monday morning, Sullivan campaign spokesman Nate Adams said that “Alaskans deserve a complete and accurate count, and we will let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified. The Division of Elections has work left to do, and we respect the Alaskans doing it. We will not be commenting on individual ballot updates or outside projections in the meantime.”
Peltola’s participation in the Senate race wasn’t a surprise: National Democrats tried to recruit her as far back as 2025, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer playing a key role.
After announcing her run for office in January, Peltola campaigned with the slogan “Fish, Family, Freedom,” emphasizing an anticorruption platform, limits on commercial trawl fisheries and a politically moderate stance that includes support for development and oil and gas drilling on federal land in Alaska.
One of 16 candidates in the August primary election, the former Alaska U.S. House Representative instantly became Sullivan’s leading challenger.
Another candidate, Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, immediately drew public attention for having the same first and last name as Senator Sullivan.
The Alaska Division of Elections ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible to run, citing irregularities in his candidacy that indicated he was running only to confuse voters, but Dan J. Sullivan appealed the decision and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in his favor.
Dan J. Sullivan finished third in the primary. Fourth-place primary election finisher David Leslie, a progressive Democrat, withdrew after the final result. That promoted Heikes into the general election and concentrated the Democratic vote around Peltola.
Republican and Democratic campaigners collectively spent more than $100 million to promote Peltola and Senator Sullivan, making it the most expensive election campaign in state history. Final tallies won’t be available until early next year.
Shortly before the primary, Peltola fired her campaign manager, Elisa Rios, and made other major staffing moves. Rios subsequently told the New York Times that Peltola was physically and verbally abusive toward staff and was a key source in a Times article that said Democratic campaigners worked to recruit independent Dan J. Sullivan as a spoiler candidate to help Peltola defeat Senator Sullivan.
Peltola herself has denied knowing about the recruitment, but Republican officials — including President Donald Trump — have called for legal action against Peltola and her campaign.
The FBI and the Alaska Department of Public Safety are investigating whether Democratic campaigners committed a legal violation. No charges have been filed.
The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil lawsuit against the Division of Elections, seeking to prevent it from certifying Peltola as the winner of the election, but a federal judge in Alaska dismissed the case. That ruling is now on appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
Part of the federal case was based on the idea that confused voters might have chosen Dan J. Sullivan instead of Senator Sullivan. Peltola now has more votes than both Sullivans combined.

sources.text:
Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in Alaska Dan Sullivan, left, and Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, right. Photos: Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff /Flickr/CC BY 2.0, Arctic Warrior / U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Moises Vasquez /Flickr/ Public Domain
(The Center Square) - Democratic candidate Mary Peltola flipped Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat, giving the party a 56-seat majority in the upper chamber beginning in January.
Peltola beat incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, with 50.1% of the vote, according to multiple media outlets. Peltola notched the victory in a four-person contest that included Daniel J. Sullivan, a schoolteacher from Petersburg, and Republican Gerald Heikes. She becomes the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the Senate since 2015.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Peltola wrote in a post on social media.
The race was called two weeks after Election Day because Alaska allows ballots to be collected up to 15 days after an election.
Democrats flipped nine seats in the U.S. Senate during the 2026 midterm elections, including in North Carolina, Ohio, Kansas and Texas. The 56-seat majority is the largest Democrats have held in the chamber since 2011. Sens. Bernie Sanders and Angus King are independents but caucus with Democrats.
Peltola focused her campaign on bringing more oil refineries to Alaska to lower gas prices, restoring federal tax credits for wind, solar and hydroelectric projects and to eliminate federal income taxes for Alaskan families making less than $92,000 per year.
The race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska was embroiled in controversy after an investigation from the New York Times alleged individuals with Peltola’s campaign sought to recruit a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Sullivan.
A spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign denied involvement in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan.
“The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in D.C.,” a spokesperson for Alaskans for Mary told The Center Square.
Peltola was first elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2022, when she became the first Alaska native to represent the state. She lost her reelection bid in 2024.
“It’s clear that the status quo in D.C. cannot go on any longer,” Peltola said in a video posted to social media. “Alaskans voted for change, and I am so honored to be your next U.S. Senator."
"Together, we’re going to put an end to the era of self-serving politicians lining their own pockets at your expense, and together we’re going to put Alaska first," she said."
Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who worked to recruit Peltola, celebrated the victory in a statement. He applauded the work of Peltola’s campaign.
“With 56 seats, Democrats are in a prime position to create a durable majority that can create lasting, real results for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

Mary Peltola Ends Democrats' 18-Year Alaska Senate Win Drought Amid DOJ 'Second Dan Sullivan' Probe
Peltola is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008, amid a DOJ probe into the alleged recruitment of a second Dan Sullivan
Mary Peltola's victory over Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan has ended an 18-year wait for a Democratic Senate election win in Alaska, but the election result has not brought an end to the controversy surrounding her campaign.
A criminal grand jury probe is examining whether people connected to Peltola's campaign or other Democratic figures helped recruit retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan to run against the incumbent in an effort to confuse voters. Peltola has denied any involvement.
Alaska's New Democratic Senator
Peltola won the closely watched contest on 17 November, securing 50.1% of the vote against Sullivan's 45.8%, according to election data. With 144,302 votes, she defeated the two-term Republican, who received 131,844.
The result gives Democrats 56 seats in the 100-member Senate when the new Congress convenes in January 2027, completing a series of nine Republican-to-Democratic seat flips in the 2026 midterm elections. Alaska was the last outstanding Senate contest to be called, with the result taking two weeks after Election Day to emerge.
Peltola previously represented Alaska in the House of Representatives and became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress.
The victory is particularly significant for Peltola, who becomes the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat elected to the chamber from Alaska since 2008.
Why Is the DOJ Investigating the 'Second Dan Sullivan'?
The controversy began when Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, entered the Alaska Senate race against Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan.
Although the two candidates had different middle initials and political affiliations, their similar names became a major talking point during the campaign. The second Sullivan qualified for the general election after finishing among the four leading candidates in Alaska's non-partisan primary.
It was subsequently reported that Democratic operatives had been involved in efforts to recruit the retired teacher as a potential challenger to the incumbent. The alleged objective was to confuse voters and divert Republican support.
