sources.text:
Republicans just absorbed one more brutal loss in a state President Trump carried three times.
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska’s U.S. Senate race, defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and flipping the final unresolved Senate seat of the 2026 midterms.
This one was close, and it was messy.
It took Alaska two full weeks to finish counting.
But the latest state results put Peltola over the 50% line, eliminating the need for a ranked-choice tabulation and handing Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority.
BREAKING: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska U.S. Senate race, flipping the seat and defeating incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.https://t.co/NNgHRHnkIi pic.twitter.com/TileMQS5A9
— The Associated Press (@AP) November 18, 2026
The numbers explain why the major election desks finally made the call.
Alaska’s Division of Elections reported Peltola with 144,302 first-choice votes, or 50.12%. Sullivan had 131,844 votes, or 45.80%, with all 401 precincts reporting in the state’s unofficial election summary and a 12,458-vote gap between them.
Two other candidates combined for fewer than 11,000 votes statewide.
One of them was Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whose similar name became a major controversy in the closing days of the race.
There were allegations that people connected to Peltola’s campaign helped recruit the second Sullivan. Those allegations fueled lawsuits, demands for investigations and a furious response from President Trump, but the official report records each Sullivan as a separate candidate with separate totals.
But Peltola’s final first-choice total makes the spoiler argument beside the point for the actual outcome. She cleared 50% without any redistribution of the other candidates’ ballots.
The report listed 287,896 votes in the Senate contest and 290,003 ballots cast statewide. It was timestamped Tuesday evening and labeled the results unofficial pending certification.
Decision Desk HQ projects Mary Peltola wins the AK US Senate General Election#DecisionMade: 10:13 PM EST
Follow live results here: https://t.co/I0LaJG41uB pic.twitter.com/9v1xHFvGu4
— Decision Desk HQ (@DecisionDeskHQ) November 18, 2026
The Associated Press said the remaining count could not realistically erase Peltola’s advantage. AP also reviewed the ranked-choice data and concluded that even if her percentage somehow slipped back below 50%, the ballots already counted showed she would still prevail comfortably in later rounds.
The call rested on more than Peltola’s narrow margin above the majority threshold. Election officials had released enough ballot-ranking information for AP to test the only plausible alternative scenario: a later ranked-choice round.
That scenario did not offer Sullivan a path. AP determined that Peltola’s lead and the known ballot preferences were sufficient to make her the winner either way, ruling out both remaining paths to a Sullivan victory.
That is the cold reality for Republicans.
The election desk had enough information to rule out both remaining paths to a Sullivan victory.
This was not a race where one technicality changed a clear winner into a loser. The GOP lost a red-state Senate seat outright.
Alaska Public Media reported that Peltola crossed the majority threshold in Tuesday’s release, meaning no ranked-choice calculation was necessary. The outlet noted that President Trump won Alaska in each of the last three presidential elections, making the Democratic flip especially painful for the GOP.
Peltola is no stranger to statewide political shocks.
She won Alaska’s lone House seat in a 2022 special election, becoming the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She lost that seat to Republican Nick Begich in 2024, then launched a comeback against Sullivan this year.
Now she is headed to the Senate, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in that chamber. Her win also returns a Democratic senator to Alaska for the first time since Mark Begich’s 2008 victory.
The state outlet also traced the race’s unusually long finish. Alaska continued reviewing absentee and other eligible ballots after Election Day, and the decisive batch released Tuesday finally carried Peltola above an outright majority.
That sequence matters because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting only when no candidate clears 50% in the first round. Once Peltola reached 50.12%, there was nothing left to redistribute.
The result therefore came from the ordinary first-choice count, not a later instant-runoff round or a disputed transfer of preferences.
The result also closes the books on a disastrous Senate cycle for Republicans.
According to The Associated Press, Democrats flipped nine GOP-held seats and will enter the next Congress with a 56-44 majority. Alaska was the final Senate contest left to resolve.
AP described Peltola’s victory as a political comeback after her 2024 House loss and noted that she defeated a two-term Republican incumbent in a state President Trump repeatedly carried by wide margins.
The report also placed the result in national context. Republicans entered the midterms with a 53-47 majority, but Democratic victories across battleground and reliably Republican states produced one of the party’s strongest Senate performances in decades.
Alaska supplied the ninth and final GOP-held seat to flip. It also gave Democrats a cushion far beyond the bare majority they needed to control the chamber.
BREAKING: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, NBC News projects, pushing her party’s Senate majority to 56 seats after a stunning wave election.https://t.co/8wtnZCW668 pic.twitter.com/Keth3qk3sh
— NBC News (@NBCNews) November 18, 2026
For conservatives, the temptation will be to focus exclusively on the controversy surrounding the second Dan Sullivan.
That controversy deserves a complete investigation. Voters should know who recruited the candidate, what promises were made and whether any campaign crossed a legal line.
But investigations cannot become an excuse for ignoring the political failure staring Republicans in the face.
Peltola won more first-choice votes than both Sullivan candidates combined. She also won more than half of every valid first-choice vote cast. The party cannot fix that by arguing over ballot transfers that never happened.
Republicans need to ask how an incumbent senator lost in a state Trump carried comfortably, why Peltola rebuilt a winning coalition after losing her House seat, and why the national GOP suffered enough defeats to turn a 53-47 Republican majority into a 56-44 Democratic one.
Those are not pleasant questions. They are necessary ones.
Alaska was supposed to be the place where Republicans survived the wave. Instead, it became the final exclamation point.
The count is in, and Peltola cleared 50%.
Sullivan lost. The Republican Party now has one more red-state defeat it cannot afford to explain away.

by Emmitt Barry, Worthy News Washington D.C. Bureau Chief
WASHINGTON, D.C. (Worthy News) – Democrats have secured a commanding 56–44 majority in the U.S. Senate after former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, completing a nine-seat Democratic pickup in the November midterm elections.
The Associated Press declared Peltola the winner Tuesday night after updated election returns showed she received 144,302 votes (50.1%) compared with Sullivan’s 131,844 votes (45.8%), a margin of 12,458 votes, or about 4.3 percentage points.
With approximately 99% of ballots counted, Peltola surpassed the 50% threshold required to win outright under Alaska’s election system, avoiding a ranked-choice tabulation.
Her victory marks the first time Alaska has elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 2008, despite the state supporting President Donald Trump in the previous three presidential elections.

Incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan has yet to concede; his campaign said he would not do so until the results were officially certified. Peltola, on the other hand, didn’t wait to celebrate – and neither did Chuck Schumer (D-NY), who still expects he’ll be the Senate majority leader come January.
“It’s official: 56 Democratic Senate seats!” Schumer posted on X Tuesday night. “Mary Peltola will be a phenomenal Senator. That’s an interesting take for the New York lawmaker, given Peltola’s platform and her own celebratory comments. In a statement, Peltola said that in electing her, voters sent a clear message that “the status quo in D.C. is not working for Alaska.” Now, it could well be that she meant the GOP’s long hold over Alaska and more recent trifecta in Washington.
But did it also apply to Schumer’s reign as party leader in the Senate? Perhaps. Peltola spent most of her campaign distancing herself from the national Democratic Party, and her ideas – at least the ones she professed during election season, anyway – aren’t the most in line with Schumer’s own beliefs.
As Schumer pointed out, she ran her platform on fish, family, and freedom. She also promoted herself as supportive of border security, gun rights, and the oil-and-gas industry. And when Republican opponents called her a supporter of transgender-friendly laws, she pushed back, responding: “No, I don’t want kids getting surgeries to change genders or men in girls’ bathrooms.”

Peltola’s win marks the ninth GOP-held Senate seat flipped by the Democrats – and 56-44 is a commanding lead. To pass legislation, Democrats only need to convince four Republican senators to cross the aisle. sources.news_title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska Senate, becomes first Alaska Native elected to US Senate
sources.text:
Mary Peltola defeated Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, becoming Alaska's first Native US senator and giving Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority.
Democrat Mary Peltola won Alaska’s US Senate race on Tuesday, projections from US media showed, defeating Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and giving her party its ninth Senate flip of the midterm elections and a commanding 56-44 majority in the upper house of Congress.
Peltola, 53, who made a living in the commercial fishing industry before entering politics, also becomes the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in her home state in nearly 20 years and the first Alaska Native ever to do so.
Alaska Natives account for roughly 15% to 18% of Alaska’s population, the highest Indigenous proportion of any US state.
Democrats secure 56-seat Senate majority
The contest was the final uncalled midterm race in the Senate. Peltola’s win gives Democrats their largest Senate majority since 2009 which, combined with securing control over the House of Representatives, sets up two years of possible deadlock between Congress and Republican President Donald Trump.
Peltola was projected to have won 50% of first-place votes to Sullivan’s 46%, enough to clear the 50% threshold and avoid additional rounds under Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system.
Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but voter frustration with the high cost of living and the state’s strong independent political streak put it back in play for Democrats.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Peltola said on X after media projected her victory. “Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who enlisted Peltola to challenge Sullivan, hailed her victory in a separate message posted on X as a “gift to Alaska, the Senate, and all of America.”
Alaska race overshadowed by candidate controversy
“It’s official: 56 Democratic Senate seats!” Schumer wrote. “Her knowledge and love for Alaska are unparalleled, and she ran a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about – fish, family, and freedom.”
Alaska’s far-flung and isolated communities can make its election counts unusually lengthy. The race was further complicated by allegations that Democrats helped recruit an independent candidate as a spoiler.
Two other candidates were on the general-election ballot: Republican Gerry Heikes, a drywall contractor, and Dan J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher running as an independent.
Republicans alleged that Sullivan Jr. was recruited to confuse voters who supported the incumbent senator and unsuccessfully sought to remove him from the ballot, arguing he was not a “good faith” candidate. Alaska’s Supreme Court rejected that argument.
Just before Election Day, the New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign had helped recruit Sullivan Jr. into the race. Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement. Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation into the allegations and has said it was examining anything that could “resemble perjury.”
The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation into possible wrongdoing. US Attorney General Todd Blanche has described the reported recruitment effort as “fraud.”
The department has sent more than 140 subpoenas, letters and notices in its investigation, Reuters previously reported, though those actions do not indicate guilt.
Peltola makes history in Alaska politics
Peltola became the first Alaska Native ever elected to Congress in 2022 in a special election to fill Alaska’s lone House seat following the death of longtime Republican incumbent Don Young.
In that race, she defeated two brand-name Alaska Republicans in an upset victory over former Governor Sarah Palin and Nick Begich III, helped by the endorsement of Alaska Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski and Young’s congressional staff. She was re-elected to a full two-year term in 2022, but lost her bid for a second full term in 2024 to Begich.
Born in Anchorage, Peltola grew up in several communities along the Kuskokwim River in southwestern Alaska. Her mother was a member of the Yup’ik group of Alaska Natives and her father was a German American who moved to Alaska from Nebraska.

Les Autochtones représentent environ 15 à 18 % de la population de l’Alaska, soit la plus forte proportion de population indigène de tous les États américains.
Grâce à cette victoire, les démocrates disposent de leur plus large majorité au Sénat depuis 2009. Comme ils ont également pris le contrôle de la Chambre des représentants, deux années de blocage potentiel s’annoncent entre le Congrès et le président républicain Donald Trump.
« La pêche, la famille et la liberté »
Selon le décompte officiel publié par les autorités de l’Etat, Mary Peltola a recueilli 50,12 %, contre 45,8 % pour Dan Sullivan. Ce score lui permet d’éviter des tours de décompte supplémentaires dans le cadre du vote préférentiel en vigueur en Alaska. Donald Trump avait remporté l’État avec 13 points d’avance en 2024. Mais l’exaspération des électeurs face à la hausse du coût de la vie, conjuguée à une forte tradition d’indépendance politique, a permis aux démocrates de redevenir compétitifs.
« En tant qu’Alaskienne de toujours, qui a consacré sa carrière au service de notre État, il n’est pas de plus grand honneur que de recevoir le soutien des Alaskiens dans notre combat contre la cupidité des grandes entreprises, pour faire baisser le coût de la vie et pour faire passer l’Alaska avant tout », a déclaré Mary Peltola sur X, après l’annonce de sa victoire par les médias. « Merci, l’Alaska. Au travail. »
We did it, Alaska! pic.twitter.com/4bDrCCl10d
— Mary Peltola (@MaryPeltola) November 18, 2026
Le chef de la minorité démocrate au Sénat, Chuck Schumer, qui l’avait convaincue d’affronter Dan Sullivan, a salué dans un autre message publié sur X une victoire qui constitue selon lui « un cadeau pour l’Alaska, pour le Sénat et pour toute l’Amérique ». « C’est officiel : 56 sièges démocrates au Sénat ! », s’est-il réjoui. « Sa connaissance de l’Alaska et son amour pour cet État sont sans égal, et elle a mené une campagne irréprochable, centrée sur les sujets qui comptent le plus pour les Alaskiens : la pêche, la famille et la liberté. »
Controverse de dernière minute
En raison de l’éloignement et de l’isolement de nombreuses communautés, le dépouillement des votes est souvent particulièrement long en Alaska. Le scrutin a en outre été compliqué par des accusations selon lesquelles les démocrates auraient contribué à recruter un candidat indépendant pour brouiller les cartes.
Deux autres candidats figuraient en effet sur le bulletin de l’élection générale : le républicain Gerry Heikes, entrepreneur en plâtrerie, et Dan J. Sullivan Jr., enseignant à la retraite se présentant comme indépendant. Les républicains ont accusé les démocrates d’avoir recruté ce dernier pour semer la confusion chez les électeurs du sénateur sortant, et ont tenté en vain de le faire retirer du bulletin au motif qu’il ne serait pas un candidat « de bonne foi ». La Cour suprême de l’Alaska a rejeté cet argument.
Peu avant le jour du scrutin, le New York Times a rapporté que l’équipe de campagne de Mary Peltola avait participé au recrutement de Dan J. Sullivan Jr., ce que celle-ci a démenti. Le gouverneur républicain Mike Dunleavy a ordonné l’ouverture d’une enquête au niveau de l’État, précisant qu’elle porterait sur tout ce qui pourrait « s’apparenter à un parjure ». Le ministère de la Justice a également ouvert une enquête pénale, le ministre Todd Blanche qualifiant de « fraude » la tentative de recrutement rapportée. D’après de précédentes informations de Reuters, le ministère a envoyé plus de 140 citations à comparaître, courriers et notifications dans le cadre de cette enquête, sans que ces démarches ne préjugent d’une quelconque culpabilité. Finalement, Mary Peltola a remporté l’élection avec près de 12 500 voix d’avance sur son adversaire républicain, tandis que l’homonyme de ce dernier en a récolté moins de 5 000.
En 2022, la démocrate était devenue la première Autochtone d’Alaska élue au Congrès, à l’issue d’une élection partielle organisée pour pourvoir l’unique siège de l’État à la Chambre des représentants après le décès de Don Young, élu républicain de longue date. Lors de ce scrutin, elle avait créé la surprise en battant deux figures républicaines bien connues en Alaska, l’ancienne gouverneure Sarah Palin et Nick Begich III, avec le soutien de la sénatrice républicaine de l’Alaska Lisa Murkowski et de l’ancienne équipe parlementaire de Don Young. Réélue la même année pour un mandat complet de deux ans, elle avait ensuite été battue par Nick Begich en 2024, alors qu’elle briguait un second mandat complet.
Née à Anchorage, Mary Peltola a grandi dans plusieurs localités situées le long du fleuve Kuskokwim, dans le sud-ouest de l’Alaska. Sa mère était membre du peuple autochtone Yup’ik, et son père, un Américain d’origine allemande, était venu du Nebraska pour s’installer en Alaska.

Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, completing a midterm sweep that will give Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority in January.
The Associated Press called the race for Peltola at about 10:19 p.m. Eastern time Tuesday, two weeks after Election Day, when a new batch of counted ballots pushed her above 50% of the vote.
That threshold let her win outright and skip Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation. The update put her ahead by 12,458 votes out of 287,896 counted, or about 4.3 percentage points, the AP explained.
Alaska was the last Senate contest of the year to be resolved. Democrats flipped nine Republican-held seats to retake the chamber, the Associated Press reported. Peltola’s win came in a state Donald Trump carried three times by double digits.
Besides Alaska, Democrats flipped seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi, Roll Call reported. The 56-seat caucus includes independents Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said in a statement reported by NBC News.
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, is a former state legislator who in 2022 became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She lost her at-large House seat in 2024 to Republican Nick Begich.
A Race Shadowed by the Second Dan Sullivan
The campaign was dogged by the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher listed on the ballot alongside the incumbent. The New York Times reported last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit him.
Peltola has denied any connection to that effort, and the second Sullivan has said running was his own decision. GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation, and the Justice Department said it would keep probing.

sources.news_title: Alaska Dem Mary Peltola Unseats Dan Sullivan as 'Decoy Dan' Ballot Scheme Hands Dems 56-Seat Senate Majority
sources.text:
Democrats have flipped their ninth Republican-held Senate seat of the 2026 midterms, with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska — a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 13 points in 2024 — according to projections reported by Fox News and POLITICO.
The result hands Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority and makes Peltola the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate, as well as the first Democrat to represent the state in the chamber since 2015, per The New York Times. POLITICO noted it is the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in Alaska.
The contest was shadowed by a controversy that broke just days before Election Day. The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides, attorneys and national Democratic operatives had taken part in a secret effort to recruit a candidate sharing the Republican incumbent's name — an operation internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," according to text messages and interviews reviewed by the Times. The reporting described discussions involving the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and talk of establishing a new right-wing political party, all aimed at recruiting candidates who could siphon votes from Sullivan.
Peltola's campaign denied involvement with either Sullivan campaign, and the DSCC also rejected allegations of participation. Republican Gov. Michael Dunleavy ordered an investigation into whether the alleged recruitment effort violated Alaska law. The status of that probe was not publicly detailed as of Tuesday.
Fox News reported the projection on X, posting: "BREAKING: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to win the Alaska Senate race, making history as the state's first Alaska Native senator. She defeats incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan after a heated campaign overshadowed by the 'Decoy Dan' ballot scandal."
Social media posts tracking the race circulated widely in the final stretch. An Instagram post indexed under the caption "Mary Peltola leads Dan Sullivan 60% to 40% in Alaska" showed campaign-related content from the contest; a separate Instagram post captioned "Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola is headed ..." documented the candidate on the trail. Neither post constitutes official results.
The Cook Political Report had rated the race a toss-up, reflecting an unusually competitive environment in a state that has generally favored Republicans in federal elections. Republicans were defending a seat in territory Trump won comfortably two years earlier, and Democrats eyed what the Times described as a rare opportunity to make inroads in traditionally Republican territory.
Peltola, a former state lawmaker, made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election to succeed the late Republican Rep. Don Young. She defeated former Republican Gov. Sarah Palin in that contest and won a full term later that year before losing her 2024 reelection bid to Republican Nick Begich III — setting up her Senate run.
Sullivan, a Marine Corps veteran and former Alaska attorney general, first won his Senate seat in 2014 by defeating Democratic incumbent Mark Begich. Newsweek reported one day before the projection that Sullivan's campaign had broken its silence in the uncalled race with a promise for the week — a statement that arrived as the decoy-candidate story consumed the final days of the contest.
The ninth GOP seat lost puts Democrats at 56 in the chamber. For Alaska voters, the immediate question is what the Dunleavy investigation finds and whether the recruitment effort described by the Times is referred for prosecution. For Republicans nationally, nine flips in a single cycle is the arithmetic of a wave, and the Senate map that Trump's second term must govern through now belongs to the opposition.
Our Take
Let's be clear about what just happened in Alaska. A state Trump won by thirteen points sent a Democrat to the Senate — and it did not happen in a vacuum. According to the Times' own reporting, campaign aides, attorneys and national operatives were involved in a scheme to put a second "Dan Sullivan" on the ballot to bleed votes from the real one. Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny it. Fine. Then they should have no objection to Governor Dunleavy's investigation running to completion and the findings being made public.
Nine seats. That is the number patriots need to sit with. The same national machine that spent years telling you the border was fine and the economy was strong just ran the table on Senate races, and in Alaska it allegedly did so with a ballot trick straight out of a banana republic playbook. The legacy media will call this a repudiation. We call it a warning: when the rules themselves become the weapon, no red state is safe, and the only answer is election integrity with teeth — real investigations, real prosecutions, real consequences.
Alaskans deserve to know who funded the "ballot composition project," who recruited the decoy, and who signed off. Until Dunleavy's probe delivers answers, every claim that this was a clean win should be treated with the skepticism it has earned. The question now is simple, folks: will anyone be held accountable, or does the machine get away with it again?

Democrats flipped 9 US Senate seats in the midterms — the most in almost 70 years
WASHINGTON (AP) - Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s competitive U.S. Senate race has flipped a ninth Republican-held seat to the Democrats, giving Peltola’s party its biggest midterm gain in nearly 70 years.
Democrats last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election in 1958, during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s second term. That year, Democrats wrested away 13 Republican-held seats and also won both of Alaska’s newly created seats, for a total gain of 15 seats.
Peltola’s victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party’s largest advantage in the Senate in 16 years. Democrats held 58 Senate seats in the waning days of the 111th Congress, which concluded on Jan. 3, 2011.
“56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said in statement posted on social media. “Most people didn’t think 51 Democratic Senate seats was a possibility at the beginning of this cycle.”
Even without Alaska, Democrats would have secured their largest majority since January 2015, when Republicans took control after flipping nine Democratic seats in the 2014 midterms during President Barack Obama’s second term.
Democrat Scott Colom’s U.S. Senate victory Wednesday in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race gave his party its eighth Republican-held seat. That win delivered Democrats their most midterm pickups since President Ronald Reagan’s second midterm election 40 years ago.
Democrats also reclaimed the House, picking up 42 seats as of Tuesday. The gains continued a historical trend of midterm losses for the president’s party.
The Senate has tended to be less susceptible to the midterm effect than the House. In seven of the last 16 midterms prior to 2026, the president’s party either held its ground or gained seats in the Senate, though all but one of those midterms occurred in the president’s first term. A president’s second midterm tends to be more punishing.
By comparison, the president’s party had gained House seats in only two midterms since the end of World War II.

Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.

The Democrats also won back the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.
Peltola defeated the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S Sullivan, who is yet to comment.
In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".
She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.
Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate, and is the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Alaska since 2008.
Donald Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but defeat for the Republicans in this year's US Senate race in the state caps off a string of losses in the midterms for the president's party.
Many voters across the United States cited cost-of-living issues as a factor that affected how they cast their ballots.

sources.news_title: Why AP called the Alaska Senate race for Democrat Mary Peltola
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Associated Press declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner in the race for U.S. Senate in Alaska on Tuesday, after an update in the vote count pushed her share of the vote above 50% — the threshold to win outright and skip the state’s ranked choice voting system.
The Tuesday update put Peltola up by 12,458 votes out of 287,896 counted, or about 4.3 percentage points over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Only a small number of ballots remain to be counted, most of which are absentee mail ballots. Peltola has handily beaten Sullivan among these last-to-be-counted ballots, which strongly suggests her vote share will remain above 50% once all ballots are added to the count.
In the unlikely event Peltola’s share of the vote falls back under 50% once the count is completed, triggering the ranked choice voting process, the ballots counted so far and data released to date by state election officials show Peltola would win comfortably in that process.
To have a chance of prevailing over Peltola in ranked choice voting, the incumbent Sullivan would need to be the second choice of essentially all voters for every other candidate -– Republican Gerald Heikes, independent Dan J. Sullivan Jr. and write-in ballots. Data already released by state election officials show that is not the case.
Officials in Alaska provide what are known as “cast vote records,” which cannot be linked to individual voters but show how each candidate was ranked on individual ballots. These records show many of the voters who didn’t rank Peltola or Sen. Sullivan as their first choice also didn’t rank anyone as their second choice, and only some of those who did make a second choice put Sen. Sullivan ahead of Peltola.
In fact, these cast vote records show that Peltola would stand to gain more votes than Sen. Sullivan after first-choice votes for write-in candidates and Dan J. Sullivan Jr. were redistributed, which would be enough to put her back above 50% and headed to Washington as the 56th Democrat in the Senate.

sources.text:
Former Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola has won Alaska’s U.S. Senate contest, toppling the Republican incumbent, according to a race call by the Associated Press.
Peltola bested Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in one of the country’s most closely watched Senate campaigns.
Election results released Tuesday show Peltola winning 50.1% of Alaskans’ first-place votes, meaning no ranked-choice calculation is needed.
Though ballots mailed from overseas have until Wednesday to arrive, the Associated Press estimates that 99% of the vote has now been counted. It has determined that Sullivan has no viable path to reelection.
The AP has not called Alaska’s U.S. House race. Congressman Nick Begich has 47.5%. Independent Bill Hill, endorsed by the Democratic Party, trails with 41.8%.
Peltola’s victory flips a Senate seat in a state that President Donald Trump carried in each of the last three presidential elections.
The race was roiled in the final days by allegations in a New York Times report that Peltola’s team was involved in recruiting another candidate in the race, Dan J. Sullivan, to try to siphon votes from the incumbent.
Peltola denied knowing about the recruitment drive, which remains the subject of state and federal investigations.
The margin of her win undercuts arguments that “decoy” candidates cost Sullivan reelection. Trump made that argument again Monday morning.
“They put in a fake candidate. They put in two fake candidates, not one. And if you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.
His information was out of date. As of Saturday’s update, Peltola’s vote count surpassed the combined sum of Sen. Sullivan, Dan J. Sullivan and Republican Gerald Heikes. She now has nearly 1,600 votes more than the total of the other three.
Peltola boosted by hostile political environment for Republicans
Peltola is the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alaska since 2008, and will be the first Alaska Native person to serve in the U.S. Senate.
Peltola campaigned mostly on the themes that Democrats around the country focused on: affordability, healthcare costs and accusing Republicans of flagrant corruption. The cost of living argument has special salience in rural Alaska, where groceries and gas can be double or triple the cost elsewhere.
With a campaign motto of “fish, family, freedom,” she also spoke of the salmon crisis on the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers, an issue that propelled her to statewide prominence in her successful U.S. House race in 2022. In this campaign, she pitched herself as the candidate who would crack down on industrial-scale pollock fishing in the Bering Sea. Alaskans increasingly blame that industry for catching and wasting salmon, halibut and other species.
Sullivan is a Marine veteran elected to the Senate in 2014. He previously served as Alaska’s attorney general. He is a strong advocate for augmenting the military and Coast Guard’s presence in Alaska.
Sullivan has also been a steadfast ally of Trump. The president flew to Wasilla last month and held a rally to boost Sullivan’s candidacy. But Trump’s approval ratings in Alaska and nationally have plunged since 2024, driven largely by opposition to the Iran War and angst over high prices.
Alaska’s election results, like those around the country, suggest that his unpopularity was a drag on Republican incumbents.
High-ranking Republicans, though, allege trickery.
Legal loose ends
Sullivan, Gov. Mike Dunleavy and federal prosecutors claim the goal of Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy was to confuse voters, robbing them of a meaningful vote, and they are pursuing the allegation on multiple fronts.
“Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” the Justice Department said before Election Day.
Peltola’s substantial lead, though, seems to nullify a U.S. Justice Department lawsuit filed Oct. 22. It sought to block certification if Sen. Sullivan lost, pending an investigation to determine if confused voters accidentally chose the wrong Sullivan, siphoning a decisive number of votes away from the senator.
The DOJ is appealing a federal judge’s dismissal of the case. The government did not seek an expedited schedule, so no decision is expected before the new Congress is sworn in.
Meanwhile, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman announced a criminal investigation into the recruitment of the other Sullivan, though he did not cite specific laws that may have been broken. Dunleavy also said he’s investigating.
Ballot-stacking and promoting spoilers is generally legal in Alaska, and has been relatively common.

Peltola’s participation in the Senate race wasn’t a surprise: National Democrats tried to recruit her as far back as 2025, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer playing a key role.
After announcing her run for office in January, Peltola campaigned with the slogan “Fish, Family, Freedom,” emphasizing an anticorruption platform, limits on commercial trawl fisheries and a politically moderate stance that includes support for development and oil and gas drilling on federal land in Alaska.
One of 16 candidates in the August primary election, the former Alaska U.S. House Representative instantly became Sullivan’s leading challenger.
Another candidate, Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, immediately drew public attention for having the same first and last name as Sen. Sullivan.
The Alaska Division of Elections ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible to run, citing irregularities in his candidacy that indicated he was running only to confuse voters, but Dan J. Sullivan appealed the decision and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in his favor.
Dan J. Sullivan finished third in the primary. Fourth-place primary election finisher David Leslie, a progressive Democrat, withdrew after the final result. That promoted Heikes into the general election and concentrated the Democratic vote around Peltola.
Republican and Democratic campaigners collectively spent more than $100 million to promote Peltola and Sen. Sullivan, making it the most expensive election campaign in state history. Final tallies won’t be available until early next year.
Shortly before the primary, Peltola fired her campaign manager, Elisa Rios, and made other major staffing moves. Rios subsequently told the New York Times that Peltola was physically and verbally abusive toward staff and was a key source in a Times article that said Democratic campaigners worked to recruit independent Dan J. Sullivan as a spoiler candidate to help Peltola defeat Sen. Sullivan.
Peltola herself has denied knowing about the recruitment, but Republican officials — including President Donald Trump — have called for legal action against Peltola and her campaign.
The FBI and the Alaska Department of Public Safety are investigating whether Democratic campaigners committed a legal violation. No charges have been filed.
The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil lawsuit against the Division of Elections, seeking to prevent it from certifying Peltola as the winner of the election, but a federal judge in Alaska dismissed the case. That ruling is now on appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
Part of the federal case was based on the idea that confused voters might have chosen Dan J. Sullivan instead of Sen. Sullivan. Peltola now has more votes than both Sullivans combined.
